facts.statement: The genus Microraptor was described by Xu and colleagues in 2000.
facts.quote: authority: Xu et al., 2000

facts.statement: Well-preserved fossils of Microraptor have been found in Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: Numerous well-preserved fossil specimens have been recovered from Liaoning, China.

facts.statement: Microraptor lived during the early Cretaceous, specifically the Aptian stage, between 125 and 120 million years ago.
facts.quote: They date from the early Cretaceous Jiufotang Formation (Aptian stage), 125 to 120 million years ago.

facts.statement: Microraptor is a small genus of four-winged dromaeosaurid dinosaurs.
facts.quote: Microraptor (Greek, μικρός, mīkros: "small"; Latin, raptor: "one who seizes") is a genus of small, four-winged dromaeosaurid dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Microraptor possessed long pennaceous feathers on its arms, tail, and legs.
facts.quote: Microraptor had long pennaceous feathers that formed aerodynamic surfaces on the arms and tail but also on the legs.

facts.statement: In 2003, Xu Xing described a Microraptor specimen as a "four-winged dinosaur" and speculated it could glide using all four limbs.
facts.quote: This led paleontologist Xu Xing in 2003 to describe the first specimen to preserve this feature as a "four-winged dinosaur" and to speculate that it may have glided using all four limbs for lift.

facts.statement: Later studies suggest Microraptor may have been capable of powered flight.
facts.quote: Subsequent studies have suggested that Microraptor was capable of powered flight as well.

facts.statement: The initial Microraptor specimen was a chimeric patchwork of different species assembled from fossils smuggled from China to the USA.
facts.quote: The first specimen to be described was part of a chimeric specimen—a patchwork of different feathered dinosaur species (Microraptor itself, Yanornis and an as-of-yet undescribed third species) assembled from multiple specimens in China and smuggled to the USA for sale.

facts.statement: Xu Xing later published a description of the tail specimen, naming it Microraptor zhaoianus.
facts.quote: However, Xu had discovered the remains of the specimen from which the tail had been taken and published a description of it later that year, giving it the name Microraptor zhaoianus.

facts.statement: Mark Norell and colleagues described an unnamed Microraptor specimen in 2002.
facts.quote: In 2002 Mark Norell et al. described another specimen, BPM 1 3-13, which they did not name or refer to an existing species.

facts.statement: Cryptovolans pauli specimens were collected from the early Albian Jiufotang Formation in Liaoning, China.
facts.quote: The type specimens of C. pauli were collected from the Jiufotang Formation, dating from the early Albian and now belong to the collection of the Paleontology Museum of Beipiao, in Liaoning, China.

facts.statement: Senter and colleagues in 2004 suggested that Cryptovolans pauli and Microraptor gui are synonyms of Microraptor zhaoianus due to individual variation.
facts.quote: In a review by Phil Senter and colleagues in 2004, the scientists suggested that all these features represented individual variation across various age groups of a single Microraptor species, making the name Cryptovolans pauli and Microraptor gui junior synonyms of Microraptor zhaoianus.

facts.statement: Some researchers accept Microraptor gui as a distinct species based on a 2013 specimen.
facts.quote: M. gui has been accepted as a distinct species with the specimen reported in 2013 being distinguishable from the type specimen of M. zhaoianus.

facts.statement: A new Microraptor specimen revealed probably glossy-black iridescent plumage.
facts.quote: A new specimen of Microraptor, BMNHC PH881, showed several features previously unknown in the animal, including the probably glossy-black iridescent plumage coloration.

facts.statement: A new specimen suggests the nuchal crest seen in the holotype may be a taphonomic artifact.
facts.quote: The new specimen also showed no sign of the nuchal crest, indicating that the crest inferred from the holotype specimen may be an artifact of taphonomic distortion.

facts.statement: Over 300 undescribed Microraptor specimens were reported in 2010, though many were altered by collectors.
facts.quote: In 2010, it was reported that there were over 300 undescribed specimens attributable to Microraptor or its close relatives among the collections of several Chinese museums, though many had been altered or composited by private fossil collectors.

facts.statement: Cryptovolans is usually considered a synonym of Microraptor.

facts.statement: Norell and colleagues described the specimen BPM 1 3-13 in 2002 as the first dinosaur known to possess flight feathers on both its legs and arms.
facts.quote: Norell et al. (2002) described BPM 1 3-13 as the first dinosaur known to have flight feathers on its legs as well as on its arms.

facts.statement: The first additional Microraptor specimens were discovered in 2001, and four more were acquired by Xu's museum between 2001 and 2003.
facts.quote: The first of these specimens was discovered in 2001, and between 2001 and 2003 four more specimens were bought from private collectors by Xu's museum, the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology.

facts.statement: The holotype of M. gui measured 77 cm in length, had a wingspan of 88 to 94 cm, and weighed between 0.5 and 1.4 kg.
facts.quote: Microraptor was among the smallest-known non-avian dinosaurs, with the holotype of M. gui measuring 77 cm in length, 88 - 94 cm in wingspan and weighing 0.5 - 1.4 kg.

facts.statement: Larger specimens of Microraptor measured at least 80 cm in length, had wingspans exceeding 99 cm, and weighed between 1.25 and 1.88 kg.
facts.quote: There are larger specimens which would have measured at least 80 cm in length, more than 99 cm in wingspan and weighed 1.25 - 1.88 kg.

facts.statement: Seven specimens of M. zhaoianus have been described in detail, providing most of the known feather impressions.
facts.quote: Seven specimens of M. zhaoianus have been described in detail, from which most feather impressions are known.

facts.statement: Microraptor had a thick body covering of feathers and a diamond-shaped fan at the end of its tail, possibly for flight stability.
facts.quote: Their bodies had a thick covering of feathers, with a diamond-shaped fan on the end of the tail (possibly for added stability during flight).

facts.statement: While some specimens show bands suggesting color patterns, at least some individuals almost certainly had iridescent black coloration.
facts.quote: Bands of dark and light present on some specimens may indicate color patterns present in life, though at least some individuals almost certainly possessed an iridescent black coloration.

facts.statement: Quanguo Li and colleagues determined the plumage coloration of Microraptor in March 2012 based on the specimen BMNHC PH881.
facts.quote: In March 2012, Quanguo Li et al. determined the plumage coloration of Microraptor based on the new specimen BMNHC PH881, which also showed several other features previously unknown in Microraptor.

facts.statement: Analysis of melanosomes in Microraptor indicated iridescent black, glossy plumage similar to that of a modern starling.
facts.quote: In Microraptor, these cells were shaped in a manner consistent with black, glossy coloration in modern birds. These rod-shaped, narrow melanosomes were arranged in stacked layers, much like those of a modern starling, and indicated iridescence in the plumage of Microraptor.

facts.statement: Xu and colleagues suggested in 2003 that basal dromaeosaurs were likely small, lived in trees, and could glide.
facts.quote: The work of Xu et al. (2003) suggested that basal dromaeosaurs were probably small, arboreal, and could glide.

facts.statement: Microraptor had long pennaceous feathers on its arms and hands measuring 10 to 20 cm, and on its legs and feet measuring 11 to 15 cm.
facts.quote: It had long pennaceous feathers on arms and hands 10 – 20 cm with legs and feet 11 – 15 cm.

facts.statement: The long feathers on Microraptor's legs were true flight feathers similar to modern birds, and asymmetrical vanes were present on its arm, leg, and tail feathers.
facts.quote: The long feathers on the legs of Microraptor were true flight feathers as seen in modern birds, with asymmetrical vanes on the arm, leg, and tail feathers.

facts.statement: Microraptor possessed primary flight feathers anchored to the hand and secondary flight feathers anchored to the arm.
facts.quote: Microraptor had both primary (anchored to the hand) and secondary (anchored to the arm) flight feathers.

facts.statement: It was originally hypothesized that Microraptor was an arboreal glider because its hindwings would have hindered ground running.
facts.quote: It was originally thought that Microraptor was a glider, and probably lived mainly in trees, because the hindwings anchored to the feet of Microraptor would have hindered their ability to run on the ground.

facts.statement: Some paleontologists suggest that feathered dinosaurs may have used their wings to parachute from trees to ambush prey as a precursor to gliding or flight.
facts.quote: Some paleontologists have suggested that feathered dinosaurs used their wings to parachute from trees, possibly to attack or ambush prey on the ground, as a precursor to gliding or true flight.

facts.statement: A 2007 study by Chatterjee and Templin found that Microraptor's combined wing surface was too narrow to parachute safely from significant heights.
facts.quote: In their 2007 study, Chatterjee and Templin tested this hypothesis as well, and found that the combined wing surface of Microraptor was too narrow to successfully parachute to the ground without injury from any significant height.

facts.statement: Chatterjee and Templin left open the possibility that Microraptor could parachute short distances between closely spaced tree branches.
facts.quote: However, the authors did leave open the possibility that Microraptor could have parachuted short distances, as between closely spaced tree branches.

facts.statement: Studies of Microraptor's anatomy suggest its limb proportions resemble modern ground birds rather than tree climbers, casting doubt on the arboreal glider hypothesis.
facts.quote: However, the idea that Microraptor was an arboreal glider relies on it to have regularly climbed or even lived in trees, when study of its anatomy have shown that its limb proportions fall in line with modern ground birds rather than climbers, and its skeleton shows none of the expected adaptations in animals specialized for climbing trees.

facts.statement: Paleontologist Stephen Czerkas argued that Microraptor was a powered flier and possibly a better flyer than Archaeopteryx.
facts.quote: Describing specimens originally referenced as a distinctive species (Cryptovolans pauli), paleontologist Stephen Czerkas argued Microraptor may have been a powered flier, and indeed possibly a better flyer than Archaeopteryx.

facts.statement: Most scientists agree that Microraptor had anatomical features for flight, but its flight was less advanced than that of birds.
facts.quote: Today, most scientists agree that Microraptor had the anatomical features expected of a flying animal, though it would have been a less advanced form of flight compared to birds.

facts.statement: Other scientists argue that Microraptor's curved shoulder girdle allowed for a nearly vertical wing upstroke, suggesting capability for true powered flight.
facts.quote: However, other scientists have argued that the shoulder girdle in some paravian theropods, including Microraptor, is curved in such a way that the shoulder joint could only have been positioned high on the back, allowing for a nearly vertical upstroke of the wing.

facts.statement: A 2024 analysis by Kiat and O'Connor found that Microraptor had remex morphologies consistent with modern flying birds, unlike anchiornithids and Caudipteryx which were secondarily flightless.
facts.quote: In 2024, Kiat and O'Connor analyzed that Mesozoic birds and Microraptor had remex morphologies that are consistent with modern volant birds, while anchiornithids and Caudipteryx were secondarily flightless.

facts.statement: Xu and colleagues suggested dromaeosaurid ancestors were small, arboreal gliders, but later discoveries of primitive dromaeosaurids with short forelimbs cast doubt on this view.
facts.quote: The work of Xu and colleagues also suggested that the ancestors of dromaeosaurids were probably small, arboreal, and capable of gliding, although later discoveries of more primitive dromaeosaurids with short forelimbs unsuitable for gliding have cast doubt on this view.

facts.statement: Studies concluded that Microraptor likely evolved flight and associated features independently of bird ancestors.
facts.quote: These studies concluded that Microraptor probably evolved flight and its associated features (fused sternum, alula, etc.) independently of the ancestors of birds.

facts.statement: In 2005, Sankar Chatterjee suggested Microraptor's forewings and hindwings were arranged like a biplane rather than overlaid like a dragonfly, as the latter was anatomically impossible.
facts.quote: Sankar Chatterjee suggested in 2005 that, in order for Microraptor to glide or fly, the forewings and hindwings must have been on different levels (as on a biplane) and not overlaid (as on a dragonfly), and that the latter posture would have been anatomically impossible.

facts.statement: Some paleontologists have doubted the biplane hypothesis for Microraptor's wing arrangement and proposed alternative configurations.
facts.quote: Some paleontologists have doubted the biplane hypothesis, and have proposed other configurations.

facts.statement: A 2010 study by Alexander et al. found that a biplane model of Microraptor was structurally deficient and required an unlikely heavy-headed weight distribution for stable gliding.
facts.quote: A 2010 study by Alexander et al. described the construction of a lightweight three-dimensional physical model used to perform glide tests. Using several hindleg configurations for the model, they found that the biplane model, while not unreasonable, was structurally deficient and needed a heavy-headed weight distribution for stable gliding, which they deemed unlikely.

facts.statement: Brougham and Brusatte concluded that Alexander's model reconstruction was inconsistent with available data and insufficient to determine Microraptor's flight pattern.
facts.quote: Brougham and Brusatte, however, concluded that Alexander's model reconstruction was not consistent with all of the available data on Microraptor and argued that the study was insufficient for determining a likely flight pattern for Microraptor.

facts.statement: Brougham and Brusatte criticized Alexander's model for having hip anatomy inconsistent with other dromaeosaurs.
facts.quote: Brougham and Brusatte criticized the anatomy of the model used by Alexander and his team, noting that the hip anatomy was not consistent with other dromaeosaurs.

facts.statement: Brougham and Brusatte argued that Alexander's model was invalid because it was based on a crushed flat specimen that did not reflect Microraptor's actual anatomy.
facts.quote: Alexander's team used a specimen of Microraptor which was crushed flat to make their model, which Brougham and Brusatte argued did not reflect its actual anatomy.

facts.statement: Hartman and colleagues suggested in 2019 that Hesperonychus is an avialan close to modern birds rather than a dromaeosaur, based on phylogenetic analyses.
facts.quote: However, Hartman and colleagues suggested that Hesperonychus is not a dromaeosaur, but actually an avialan close to modern birds like Balaur bondoc based on phylogenetic analyses in 2019.

facts.statement: Scientists suggest Microraptor would have been awkward on the ground due to its extensive hindwing feathers covering most of its foot.
facts.quote: Due to the extent of the hindwings onto most of the animal's foot, many scientists have suggested that Microraptor would have been awkward during normal ground movement or running.

facts.statement: Microraptor's front wing feathers likely hindered ground movement because of limited wrist motion and extreme feather length.
facts.quote: The front wing feathers would also have hindered Microraptor when on the ground, due to the limited range of motion in the wrist and the extreme length of the wing feathers.

facts.statement: Chatterjee and Templin noted that it is equally possible that bird flight evolved through a four-winged stage or via a side branch like Microraptor that left no descendants.
facts.quote: Chatterjee and Templin did not take a strong stance on this possibility, noting that both a conventional interpretation and a tetrapteryx stage are equally possible.

facts.statement: In 2010, researchers announced the discovery of probable gut contents in the type fossil of Microraptor zhaoianus, with a full study published in 2022 by David Hone and colleagues.
facts.quote: In 2010 researchers announced that further preparation of the type fossil of M. zhaoianus revealed preserved probable gut contents, and a full study on them was later published in 2022 by David Hone and colleagues.

facts.statement: The mammal prey in the Microraptor gut contents had an estimated snout-to-vent length of 80 mm and a mass of 13–43 g.
facts.quote: The foot skeleton is similar to those of Eomaia and Sinodelphys. It corresponds to an animal with an estimated snout to vent length of 80 mm and a mass of 13 – 43 g.

facts.statement: It is ambiguous whether Microraptor preyed on or scavenged the mammal found in its gut, though the lack of other body parts suggests the foot may have been consumed during late-stage carcass scavenging.
facts.quote: It is ambiguous whether the mammal had been predated upon or scavenged by Microraptor, although the lack of other definitive body parts consumed may suggest the low-muscle mass foot may have been eaten during a late stage of carcass consumption, possibly through scavenging.

facts.statement: In December 2011, Jingmai O'Connor and coauthors described a Microraptor gui specimen containing bones of an arboreal enantiornithean bird, including a partial wing and feet, in its abdomen.
facts.quote: In the 6 December 2011 issue of Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Jingmai O'Connor and coauthors described a specimen of Microraptor gui containing bones of an arboreal enantiornithean bird in its abdomen, specifically a partial wing and feet.

facts.statement: O'Connor and coauthors interpreted the presence of a bird in a Microraptor gui specimen as evidence that Microraptor caught and consumed the bird in trees rather than scavenging it.
facts.quote: Their position implies the bird was swallowed whole and head-first, which the authors interpreted as implying that the Microraptor had caught and consumed the bird in the trees, rather than scavenging it.

facts.statement: Researchers proposed that Microraptor gui was also an adept hunter of fish, contradicting the prior suggestion that it hunted only in arboreal environments.
facts.quote: The authors contradicted the prior suggestion that M. gui hunted only in an arboreal environment, proposing that it was also an adept hunter of fish as well.

facts.statement: Researchers pointed to the first three teeth of the Microraptor gui mandible being inclined anterodorsally as evidence of probable adaptation to a fish-eating diet.
facts.quote: They further argued that the specimen showed a probable adaptation to a fish-eating diet, pointing to the first three teeth of the mandible being inclined anterodorsally, a characteristic often associated with piscivory.

facts.statement: Hone and colleagues (2022) questioned the reliability of predation interpretations for gut contents, suggesting they could equally be attributed to scavenging.
facts.quote: However, Hone and colleagues (2022) questioned the reliability of these interpretations and wrote that both could just as equally be attributed to scavenging.

facts.statement: Hone and colleagues argued that Microraptor was a generalist hunter rather than a specialist in arboreal or aquatic hunting, citing a broad range of vertebrate gut contents.
facts.quote: Further, they argued against Microraptor being a specialist in either or both arboreal or aquatic hunting, citing the broad range of vertebrate gut contents (i.e. fish, mammals, lizards, birds) as evidence for a generalist hunting strategy, and that neither required that Microraptor being a specialist for hunting in either habitats.

facts.statement: Microraptor likely passed indigestible fur, feathers, and bone bits in its droppings instead of producing gastric pellets.
facts.quote: This suggests that Microraptor passed indigestible fur, feathers, and bits of bone in its droppings instead of producing pellets.

facts.quote: Based on the morphology of the scleral ring of the eye, it has been suggested Microraptor hunted at night. However, the discovery of dark and glossy plumage in Microraptor may suggest otherwise, as no modern birds with comparable plumage are known to be nocturnal.
